cards.explain: Botrytized aszú berries are soaked in base wine or must, giving luscious, high-acid wines that live for decades.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to its method
cards.explain: Three different routes to sweetness.

cards.title: Fortified mid-fermentation
cards.body: Port comes from Portugal's **Douro Valley**. Halfway through fermentation, **grape spirit** is added. This kills the yeast, leaving a **sweet, strong (about 20% abv)**, deeply colored wine.

cards.title: Ruby vs tawny
cards.body:
- **Ruby** styles (Ruby, Reserve, LBV, Vintage): aged to keep fresh black fruit.
- **Tawny** styles: aged for years in small casks, becoming brownish with nutty, caramel notes.

cards.q: When is grape spirit added to Port?
cards.explain: Adding spirit early stops fermentation and keeps the natural grape sugar.

cards.q: Port comes from which river valley?
cards.explain: Grapes grow on steep schist terraces; wines were traditionally shipped down to Porto's lodges in Vila Nova de Gaia.

cards.q: Tawny Port gets its nutty flavors from long ageing in small wooden casks.
cards.explain: Oxygen through the small casks turns the wine tawny and develops walnut, toffee and caramel notes.

cards.q: Port is typically about ___% alcohol.
cards.explain: Usually 19–22% abv.

cards.title: The world's most misunderstood wine
cards.body:
Sherry comes from the hot south of Spain around **Jerez**. Most is made from **Palomino** and is **dry**.

- **Fino & Manzanilla**: aged under **flor** (a layer of yeast); pale, bone dry, tangy, almond and bread.
- **Oloroso**: aged with oxygen; dark, nutty, dry.
- **Pedro Ximénez**: from sun-dried grapes; black, raisiny, very sweet.

cards.title: The solera
cards.body: Sherry ages in a **solera**, tiers of barrels where younger wine gradually refreshes older wine. The result is consistent year after year, so most Sherry has no vintage.

cards.q: What is flor?
options: A layer of yeast that protects Fino from oxygen
cards.explain: It grows on the wine's surface in partly filled barrels, keeping it pale and adding bready, salty notes.

cards.q: Most Sherry is sweet.
cards.explain: Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado and Oloroso are naturally dry. Sweet styles are Pedro Ximénez, Moscatel and blended Cream Sherry.

cards.q: Which Sherry is darkest and sweetest?
cards.explain: PX is made from sun-dried grapes: syrupy, raisined and almost black.

cards.q: Manzanilla is a Fino-style Sherry aged in which seaside town?
cards.explain: Sea air helps flor grow thickly, giving an extra-salty tang.

cards.q: Sherry is aged in a fractional blending system called a ___.
cards.explain: Wine is drawn from the oldest tier and replaced from the next-oldest, and so on.

lessons.title: Deep dive: how sweetness is made

cards.title: Concentrate the sugar
cards.body:
Sweet wine needs grapes so sugary that yeast cannot (or is not allowed to) ferment it all. Four ways:

- **Noble rot** (*Botrytis cinerea*): misty mornings, sunny afternoons; the fungus pierces skins and water evaporates. Sauternes, Tokaji, Trockenbeerenauslese.
- **Drying**: grapes dry on mats or in lofts (*appassimento*, *passito*). Recioto, Vin Santo.
- **Freezing**: grapes freeze on the vine; water stays behind as ice when pressed. Icewine, Eiswein.
- **Late harvest**: simply leave grapes to shrivel on the vine.

cards.title: Icewine
cards.body:
Grapes must be picked frozen, at about **-8 °C** or colder, usually at night in December or January. Only a few drops of syrupy juice come from each bunch.

Canada (Ontario, often **Vidal** or Riesling) and Germany/Austria (Eiswein) are the leaders. The style is intensely sweet with piercing acidity.

cards.title: Stop the fermentation
cards.body:
Another route is to **stop** fermentation while sugar remains:
- Chilling and filtering out the yeast (Moscato d'Asti, many German Kabinett and Spätlese).
- Adding grape spirit, which kills the yeast: **fortification** (Port, Vins Doux Naturels).

cards.title: Tokaji Aszú
cards.body:
In Hungary's Tokaj, botrytized **aszú** berries (mainly **Furmint**) are picked one by one and soaked in fermenting wine. Sweetness used to be measured in **puttonyos**, the baskets of aszú added; today the minimum is 120 g/L of sugar.

**Eszencia** is the free-run syrup alone: so sweet it barely ferments, reaching just a few % alcohol.

cards.q: What does noble rot do to grapes?
options: Shrivels them and concentrates sugar and acid
cards.explain: Botrytis pierces the skin and water evaporates; it also adds honey, marmalade and saffron notes.

cards.q: How cold must grapes be for icewine?
cards.explain: At that temperature most of the water is frozen, leaving concentrated juice.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to its method
cards.explain: Four different routes to sweetness.

cards.q: Furmint is the main grape of Tokaji.
cards.explain: Furmint's high acidity balances the huge sweetness; Hárslevelű is its partner.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Port, Sherry and Madeira

cards.title: Port: the Douro and Gaia
cards.body:
Port grapes (Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz and others) grow on steep **schist terraces** of the Douro. Fermentation lasts only two or three days before **grape spirit at 77%** is added, leaving a sweet wine of about **19–22%**.

Traditionally the young wine went downriver to the lodges of **Vila Nova de Gaia**, opposite Porto, to age.

cards.title: Ruby or tawny?
cards.body:
- **Ruby styles** age in big vats or bottle; fruit stays deep red and fresh. Ruby, Reserve, LBV (4–6 years in wood), and **Vintage Port**, made only in declared years and aged for decades in bottle.
- **Tawny styles** age in small casks; oxygen fades the color to amber and builds nutty, caramel notes. 10, 20, 30, 40 Year Old, and **Colheita** (single harvest).

cards.title: Sherry: flor or no flor
cards.body:
Sherry is made from **Palomino** in the chalky *albariza* soils around **Jerez**. The base wine is dry; it is fortified and aged in a **solera**, a stack of casks where young wine refreshes older wine.

- **Fino / Manzanilla**: fortified to about 15%, so a layer of yeast, **flor**, grows on top and protects it from air. Pale, salty, bone dry.
- **Oloroso**: fortified to about 17%, too strong for flor; ages with oxygen into a dark, nutty wine.
- **Amontillado** and **Palo Cortado** sit in between.
- **Pedro Ximénez**: sun-dried grapes, syrupy sweet.

cards.title: Madeira: cooked and immortal
cards.body:
On the Portuguese island of Madeira, wines are deliberately **heated**: in tanks (*estufagem*) or for years in warm attics (*canteiro*). The result tastes of caramel and walnut with soaring acidity, and can last for centuries once opened.

Styles follow the grapes, dry to sweet: **Sercial**, **Verdelho**, **Bual**, **Malmsey** (Malvasia).

cards.q: Why is fino sherry so pale?
options: A layer of flor yeast protects it from oxygen
It is made from white grapes only
cards.explain: Without air contact, it stays pale and fresh, with salty, bready notes.

cards.q: Where do the big Port houses traditionally age their wines?
cards.explain: Across the Douro from Porto; the lodges' signs line the riverfront.

cards.q: Match the Madeira style to its sweetness
cards.explain: The grape names on the label tell you the sweetness.

cards.q: Tawny Port gets its color from ageing in small casks.
cards.explain: Slow oxidation turns the red to amber-brown.

cards.q: A tiered system of casks where young sherry refreshes older sherry is a ___.
cards.explain: Wine is drawn from the oldest casks and topped up from the next oldest.

cards.title: Three roads to sweetness
cards.body:
1. **Noble rot** (botrytis) shrivels grapes and concentrates sugar: Sauternes, Tokaji.
2. **Freezing**: grapes picked frozen give Icewine/Eiswein.
3. **Drying**: grapes dried after picking make Recioto and Vin Santo.

Stopping fermentation early, as in Port, is a fourth route.

cards.title: Sherry styles
cards.body: **Fino** and **Manzanilla** age under a layer of yeast called **flor**: pale, dry, salty, almond. **Oloroso** ages without flor, in contact with air: dark, nutty, dry. **Pedro Ximénez** is a dark, raisin-sweet dessert sherry.

cards.q: What is 'flor' in sherry-making?
options: A layer of yeast on the wine
cards.explain: Flor protects Fino and Manzanilla from oxygen and gives a tangy, bready, almond character.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to how it's made
cards.explain: Different routes to sugar create very different sweet wines.

cards.q: Oloroso sherry ages under flor.
cards.explain: Oloroso is fortified to a strength where flor can't survive, so it ages oxidatively and darkens.

cards.q: Which wine is fortified during fermentation, keeping natural sweetness?
cards.explain: Adding grape spirit stops fermentation, leaving sugar in the wine.

cards.q: Noble rot is caused by a fungus called ___.
cards.explain: Botrytis cinerea, in the right conditions, shrivels grapes and concentrates sugar and acid.

units.title: Reading labels
units.summary: Place versus grape, quality categories and the label terms that matter.

cards.title: Two ways to name a wine
cards.body:
- **Old World** labels often name the **place**: Chablis, Rioja, Barolo. You are expected to know the grape.
- **New World** labels usually name the **grape**: Napa Cabernet Sauvignon, Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.q: Match the place-name wine to its grape
cards.explain: Learning these 'translations' unlocks most European wine lists.

cards.q: Red Burgundy is made from…
cards.explain: And white Burgundy is Chardonnay.

cards.q: In the USA, a wine labeled 'Merlot' must contain at least 75% Merlot.
cards.explain: US law requires at least 75% of the named variety (the EU usually requires 85%).

cards.q: Which country is considered New World?
cards.explain: New World countries include the USA, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Chile and Argentina.

cards.title: The EU system
cards.body:
European wine law has two main tiers:

- **PDO** (Protected Designation of Origin): strict rules on area, grapes, yields and methods. *AOC/AOP* in France, *DOC/DOCG* in Italy, *DO/DOCa* in Spain.
- **PGI** (Protected Geographical Indication): a wider area and more flexibility. *IGP / Vin de Pays*, *IGT*, *Vino de la Tierra*.

cards.q: Which is Italy's highest wine category?
cards.explain: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, above DOC and IGT.

cards.q: PGI wines have stricter rules than PDO wines.
cards.explain: PDO is stricter. PGI allows more freedom, which is why some ambitious producers choose it (as with early Super Tuscans).

cards.q: Match the label term to its country
cards.explain: Each country has its own names for the EU PDO category.

cards.q: In Spain, Rioja and Priorat hold the top category, DOCa, also written ___ in Catalan.
cards.explain: Priorat uses the Catalan form, Denominació d'Origen Qualificada.

cards.title: Useful label terms
cards.body:
- **Vintage**: the harvest year.
- **Classico** (Italy): the historic heart of a region.
- **Riserva / Reserva**: aged longer before release.
- **Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva** (Spain): rising minimum ageing.
- **Grand Cru / Premier Cru**: top vineyard classifications (France).
- **Trocken**: dry (Germany). **Brut**: dry sparkling.

cards.q: On a Spanish label, which term means the longest ageing?
cards.explain: Red Rioja Gran Reserva: at least five years, two in oak.

cards.q: What does 'Classico' mean on an Italian label?
options: From the historic heart of the region
cards.explain: Chianti Classico is the original Chianti zone between Florence and Siena.

cards.q: The vintage on a label is the year the wine was bottled.
cards.explain: Vintage is the year the grapes were harvested.

cards.q: On a German label, ___ means dry.
cards.explain: Halbtrocken means off-dry. Spätlese is a ripeness level, not a sweetness term.

cards.title: Quality pyramids
cards.body: Most EU countries rank wines in a pyramid: **PDO** wines from tightly defined places with strict rules (AOC, DOC, DOCG, DO), **PGI** wines from wider areas with more freedom (IGP, IGT, Vino de la Tierra) and simple **wine** without a place.

cards.title: Ageing terms
cards.body: Spanish and Italian labels often show ageing: **Crianza**, **Reserva** and **Gran Reserva** in Spain; **Riserva** in Italy. Each means a longer minimum time in barrel and bottle before release.

cards.q: Which Spanish term means the longest minimum ageing?
cards.explain: For reds, Gran Reserva means at least five years of ageing, with time in oak.

cards.q: Match the label term to its country
cards.explain: Each country has its own words for top-quality, place-based wines.

cards.q: PGI wines have stricter rules than PDO wines.
cards.explain: PDO is the stricter, more specific category; PGI allows wider areas and more grapes.

cards.q: What does 'Riserva' on an Italian label tell you?
cards.explain: Riserva wines meet a longer minimum ageing period set by each DOC/DOCG.

cards.q: In Germany, a dry Prädikatswein is labeled ___.
cards.explain: Trocken means dry; Spätlese and Auslese describe ripeness at harvest, not sweetness.

units.title: Label decoder
units.summary: Read any bottle: how France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Portugal and the New World label their wines.

cards.title: Château first, place second
cards.body: A Bordeaux label names the **château** (the estate), the **appellation** and often a **classification** such as *Grand Cru Classé en 1855*. There's no grape on the front: it's a blend.

cards.title: In Burgundy, the vineyard is king
cards.body: Burgundy's hierarchy shows in the name: **Bourgogne** (regional) → **village** (Gevrey-Chambertin) → **Premier Cru** (village + vineyard) → **Grand Cru** (the vineyard alone, e.g. *Chambertin*).

cards.q: On a Bordeaux label, 'Mis en bouteille au château' means…
cards.explain: Estate bottling means the wine was made and bottled where the grapes were grown.

cards.q: Which Burgundy label shows a Grand Cru?
cards.explain: Grand Crus appear on their own name. The village name alone (Gevrey-Chambertin) is village level.

cards.q: Red Burgundy labels usually state 'Pinot Noir' on the front.
cards.explain: Place, not grape: red Burgundy is understood to be Pinot Noir, and white is Chardonnay.

cards.q: Match the Burgundy label to its level
cards.explain: The more precise the place, the higher the level.

cards.title: Champagne codes
cards.body: Look for the **house**, the **style** (Blanc de Blancs, Rosé), the **sweetness** (Brut, Extra Brut…) and the tiny **maker code**: **NM** (a house buying grapes), **RM** (a grower making their own), **CM** (a co-operative).

cards.title: Alsace names the grape
cards.body: Unusually for France, Alsace puts the **grape** first. *Grand Cru* plus a vineyard name marks the 51 best sites; *Vendanges Tardives* and *Sélection de Grains Nobles* signal sweet wines.

cards.q: What does 'RM' on a Champagne label tell you?
options: A grower made it from their own grapes
cards.explain: Récoltant-Manipulant: 'grower Champagne'.

cards.q: On a Champagne label, ___ ___ means it was made only from Chardonnay.
cards.explain: 'White from whites'. Blanc de Noirs is white wine from black grapes.

cards.q: Alsace wines are usually labeled with the grape variety.
cards.explain: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat are the classic four.

cards.title: German labels
cards.body: Expect a lot of information: **region**, **village + vineyard** (*Wehlener Sonnenuhr*), **grape** and the **Prädikat** ripeness level (Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese…). **Trocken** means dry.

cards.title: Italy and Spain
cards.body:
- **Italy**: denomination (Chianti Classico, Barolo), category **DOCG/DOC/IGT**, and ageing terms (*Riserva*, *Gran Selezione*).
- **Spain**: region (Rioja) and the ageing ladder **Joven → Crianza → Reserva → Gran Reserva**. *Cosecha* = vintage.

cards.title: Port
cards.body: The style is everything: **Ruby**, **LBV**, **Vintage**, or **Tawny** with an age (10, 20, 30, 40 years).

cards.q: On 'Wehlener Sonnenuhr', what is Sonnenuhr?
cards.explain: Wehlen is the village (adding -er), Sonnenuhr ('sundial') the vineyard.

cards.q: Which Spanish term means the longest ageing?
cards.explain: Red Rioja Gran Reserva: at least five years, two in oak. Cosecha just means vintage.

cards.q: Match the label word to its meaning
cards.explain: A small vocabulary unlocks most European labels.

cards.q: A '20 Years Old Tawny' Port is made only from wine harvested exactly 20 years ago.
cards.explain: It's an indication of age: a blend whose character matches about 20 years in cask.

cards.title: Brand, grape, place
cards.body:
New World labels lead with the **brand** and the **grape**, then the region: an **AVA** in the USA, a **GI** in Australia, **WO** in South Africa.

In the USA, a named grape means ≥75% of it, a named AVA ≥85% of grapes from there, a vintage ≥95% from that year.

cards.title: Words without legal meaning
cards.body: "Reserve", "Old Vine" and "Special Selection" usually have **no legal definition** in the New World. They're the producer's own promise.

cards.q: On a US label, a named AVA means at least what share of grapes came from there?
cards.explain: For a named grape the US minimum is 75%; for an AVA, 85%.

cards.q: 'Reserve' on a Californian wine is a legally defined quality level.
cards.explain: It's a producer term. In Spain and Italy, Reserva/Riserva *are* legally defined.

cards.q: What does GI stand for on an Australian label?
cards.explain: Australia's system of zones, regions and subregions.

cards.title: Château, Domaine, Bodega
cards.body: The producer's name often starts with a word for estate: **Château** (Bordeaux), **Domaine** (Burgundy and elsewhere in France), **Bodega** (Spain), **Weingut** (Germany, Austria), **Quinta** (Portugal) and **Tenuta** (Italy).

cards.title: Burgundy's ladder
cards.body: Burgundy labels climb a ladder: **Bourgogne** (regional), **village** (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin), **Premier Cru** (a named vineyard plus the village) and **Grand Cru** (the vineyard name alone, e.g. Chambertin).

cards.q: On a Burgundy label, which level shows only the vineyard name?
cards.explain: Grand Crus are so famous they stand alone: Montrachet, Chambertin, Romanée-Conti.

cards.q: Match the estate word to its country
cards.explain: Knowing these words helps you find the producer on any label.

cards.q: 'Mis en bouteille au château' means bottled at the estate.
cards.explain: Estate bottling shows the same property grew the grapes and bottled the wine.

cards.q: In Germany, which word tells you about ripeness at harvest?
cards.explain: Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese are Prädikat levels based on grape ripeness.

cards.q: In Rioja, a wine aged at least two years, one in oak, is labeled ___.
cards.explain: Crianza red Rioja spends at least two years ageing, with at least one in oak.

units.title: Viticulture in depth
units.summary: Site selection, training and pruning, vineyard threats, yields and harvest decisions.

cards.title: Temperature is king
cards.body:
The growing season needs a mean temperature of roughly **13–21 °C**. Growers fine-tune heat with:

- **Latitude**: further from the equator is cooler.
- **Altitude**: about 0.6 °C cooler per 100 m.
- **Aspect**: slopes facing the equator get more sunlight.
- **Water bodies**: oceans, lakes and rivers moderate extremes and reflect light.
- **Diurnal range**: cool nights preserve acidity and aroma.

cards.title: Sunlight, wind and fog
cards.body: Coastal fog and wind cool California's Sonoma Coast and Carneros, while inland Napa warms up. Chile's Humboldt Current and South Africa's Benguela Current do the same.

cards.q: Why is a large diurnal range valuable?
options: Cool nights preserve acidity and aromas
It speeds up ripening at night
cards.explain: Warm days ripen sugar; cool nights slow the loss of acid. High-altitude Argentina and Washington State rely on it.

cards.q: Approximately how much does temperature drop per 100 m of altitude?
cards.explain: So a vineyard at 1,000 m is about 6 °C cooler than one at sea level, other things being equal.

cards.q: The cold Humboldt Current cools Chile's coastal vineyards.
cards.explain: It brings cool air and morning fog to regions like Casablanca and San Antonio.

cards.q: In the Southern Hemisphere, the warmest slopes face ___.
cards.explain: Slopes facing the equator get the most direct sun: south in the Northern Hemisphere, north in the Southern.

cards.title: Shaping the vine
cards.body:
- **Bush vines** (gobelet): free-standing, low, for hot, dry, windy sites (Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Barossa old vines).
- **Cane pruning** (e.g. Guyot): one or two long canes tied to a wire each year (Burgundy, Bordeaux).
- **Spur pruning** (cordon): short spurs on a permanent arm, easier to mechanize.
- **VSP**: shoots trained upwards between wires for an even, sunny canopy.

cards.title: Canopy management
cards.body: Leaf removal, shoot positioning and trimming balance **sunlight** on the grapes (for ripeness and color) with **shade** (to prevent sunburn), and improve **airflow** to reduce disease.

cards.q: Bush vines are best suited to…
cards.explain: Low and sturdy with their own shade, they need no trellis and little water, as in the Southern Rhône and Spain.

cards.q: Guyot is a cane-pruned training system.
cards.explain: Single or double Guyot is common in Burgundy and Bordeaux.

cards.q: Which is a main aim of canopy management?
options: Balancing sunlight and airflow around the grapes
cards.explain: Good exposure helps ripening and color; airflow reduces fungal disease.

cards.q: Shoots trained vertically upward between wires is called ___.
cards.explain: Vertical Shoot Positioning, widely used in the New World and much of Europe.

cards.title: Pests and diseases
cards.body:
- **Phylloxera**: an aphid-like louse that kills vine roots. Grafting onto **American rootstock** is the main defense.
- **Powdery mildew** (oidium) and **downy mildew**: fungal diseases.
- **Grey rot** (botrytis in wet weather): destroys bunches.
- **Viruses**, birds and animals.

cards.title: Weather hazards
cards.body:
- **Spring frost** kills young shoots: use wind machines, heaters or sprinklers.
- **Hail** shreds leaves and bunches: use nets.
- **Drought** and **heatwaves** stop ripening or sunburn grapes.
- **Rain at harvest** dilutes and rots grapes.

cards.q: How do most vineyards protect against phylloxera?
cards.explain: American vine species tolerate the louse on their roots. European vines are grafted on top.

cards.q: Sprinklers can protect buds from spring frost.
cards.explain: As water freezes on the buds it releases heat, holding them at about 0 °C inside a protective ice shell.

cards.q: Which region has never been affected by phylloxera?
cards.explain: Protected by the Andes, the Atacama Desert, the Pacific and Patagonian ice, Chile has never had it. South Australia is also free.

cards.q: Match the hazard to the defense
cards.explain: Growers combine many tools to protect a year's crop.

cards.title: Less is often more
cards.body:
Lower **yields** often mean more concentrated grapes, especially from **old vines**. But very low yields are not always better, and balance matters.

Harvest timing balances **sugar**, **acidity**, **tannin ripeness** and **flavor**. Pick early for freshness and sparkling base wines; pick late for richness or sweet wines.

cards.title: Hand or machine?
cards.body:
- **Hand harvesting**: selective, gentle, keeps whole bunches (essential for Champagne and carbonic maceration); slow and costly.
- **Machine harvesting**: fast and cheap, can pick at night when it's cool; less selective, needs flat land and trellised vines.

cards.q: Why are grapes for sparkling base wine picked early?
options: To keep high acidity and moderate alcohol
cards.explain: Fresh, high-acid, relatively neutral base wines are ideal, since the second fermentation adds more alcohol.

cards.q: Machine harvesters can work at night, when grapes are cool.
cards.explain: Night picking keeps fruit fresh and reduces oxidation, which is useful in hot regions.

cards.q: Which wine style requires whole bunches, so hand harvesting is essential?
cards.explain: Whole-bunch pressing gives clean, pale juice. Champagne rules require hand harvesting.

cards.q: Vines that are decades old usually give lower ___ of more concentrated fruit.
cards.explain: 'Old vines' (vieilles vignes) is a common label term, though it has no legal definition in most places.

lessons.title: Deep dive: farming philosophies and climate change

cards.title: Organic, biodynamic, sustainable
cards.body:
- **Organic**: no synthetic herbicides, pesticides or fertilizers. Copper and sulfur are allowed against mildew.
- **Biodynamic**: organic plus a whole-farm system from Rudolf Steiner's 1924 lectures: herbal preparations and a calendar following the moon. Followers include Domaine Leflaive and Zind-Humbrecht.
- **Sustainable**: certified programs balancing environment, people and cost (Napa Green, Sustainable Wine South Africa, HVE in France).

cards.title: Yield and quality
cards.body:
Yields are measured in **hectoliters per hectare** (hl/ha). Grand Cru Burgundy is limited to about 35 hl/ha; bulk vineyards can exceed 150.

Lower yields often mean more concentrated grapes, but a healthy, balanced vine matters more than any number. Old vines naturally give small crops of small berries.

cards.title: Climate change in the vineyard
cards.body:
Harvests in Europe now come two to three weeks earlier than in the 1980s. Riper grapes mean **higher alcohol** and **lower acidity**.

Growers respond by planting on **higher, cooler sites**, facing slopes away from the sun, keeping more leaves for shade, and trying heat-tolerant grapes. England, Tasmania and southern Chile are booming as cool places get warm enough.

cards.q: What does biodynamic farming add to organic farming?
options: Herbal preparations and a lunar calendar
cards.explain: It treats the vineyard as a self-sustaining farm organism.

cards.q: How is yield usually measured?
cards.explain: 1 hl = 100 liters, or about 133 standard bottles.

cards.q: Climate change has made European harvests later.
cards.explain: They now start two to three weeks earlier than in the 1980s.

cards.title: Training and canopy
cards.body:
Vines are trained to control sun and air. **Bush vines** (gobelet) suit hot, dry places such as old Grenache in Châteauneuf. **Trellised** systems like Guyot and VSP spread leaves for sun in cool climates.

Removing leaves around the bunches improves ripening and airflow, cutting disease.

cards.title: Threats in the vineyard
cards.body:
**Phylloxera**, a root-eating aphid, destroyed most of Europe's vineyards in the late 1800s. The fix: graft vines onto American rootstock.

Fungal diseases like **powdery** and **downy mildew** thrive in damp weather; **grey rot** spoils grapes unless conditions turn it into noble rot.

cards.q: How did growers defeat phylloxera?
cards.explain: American vine roots resist phylloxera, so European vines are grafted onto them.

cards.q: Bush vines are typical of hot, dry vineyards.
cards.explain: The leafy bush shades the grapes from harsh sun; they are common in the southern Rhône, Spain and Australia.

cards.q: Match the threat to what it attacks
cards.explain: Growers fight each threat in a different way.

cards.q: Why do growers remove leaves around the bunches in cool climates?
options: More sun and air on the grapes
To make the vine grow taller
cards.explain: Exposure helps ripening and reduces rot, but too much can sunburn grapes.

cards.q: Phylloxera is a tiny insect that feeds on vine ___.
cards.explain: It sucks sap from the roots and slowly kills un-grafted European vines.

units.title: Winemaking in depth
units.summary: Before, during and after fermentation: the choices that define style.

cards.title: Preparing the must
cards.body:
- **Sorting**: removing rotten or unripe fruit.
- **Destemming and crushing**, or keeping whole bunches.
- **SO₂**: added to protect against oxygen and bacteria.
- **Must adjustments**: in cool places, **chaptalization** (adding sugar to raise alcohol); in hot places, **acidification**.
- **Cold soak**: macerating black grapes before fermentation for color and fruit.

cards.q: What is chaptalization?
options: Adding sugar to the must to raise alcohol
cards.explain: Named after Jean-Antoine Chaptal. It is allowed in cooler regions such as Burgundy and Germany (with limits) and banned in many warm regions.

cards.q: Acidification is most common in hot regions.
cards.explain: Grapes from hot climates lose acidity as they ripen, so winemakers add tartaric acid to restore balance.

cards.q: Why is sulfur dioxide (SO₂) used in winemaking?
cards.explain: Small amounts protect wine from oxidation and spoilage. Almost all wines contain some.

cards.q: Soaking black grapes before fermentation at low temperature is called a cold ___.
cards.explain: Popular for Pinot Noir to extract color and fruit before alcohol forms.

cards.title: Extraction methods
cards.body:
- **Punch down** (pigeage) and **pump over** (remontage) control extraction.
- **Whole-bunch** fermentation adds fragrance, spice and structure.
- **Carbonic maceration** gives soft, fruity reds with kirsch and banana.
- **Fermentation temperature**: cooler for fruit, warmer for extraction.
- **Vessel**: steel, oak, concrete or clay (amphora, qvevri).

cards.q: Carbonic maceration is most associated with…
cards.explain: Whole bunches in a CO₂-filled vessel give juicy, low-tannin wine with banana and bubblegum notes.

cards.q: Pigeage means punching the cap down into the wine.
cards.explain: Traditional in Burgundy, sometimes even done by foot.

cards.q: Which vessel has been used for winemaking in Georgia for about 8,000 years?
cards.explain: Large egg-shaped clay jars buried underground. Georgian qvevri winemaking is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

cards.q: Fermenting with stems attached is called whole-___ fermentation.
cards.explain: Popular for Pinot Noir and Syrah, adding aromatic lift and tannin.

cards.title: Finishing the wine
cards.body:
- **Maturation**: in steel (fresh), old oak (gentle oxygen) or new oak (flavor).
- **Blending**: varieties, vineyards, barrels.
- **Clarification**: racking, **fining** (bentonite, egg white) and **filtration**.
- **Stabilization**: cold stabilization prevents harmless tartrate crystals.
- **Closure**: natural cork, screwcap, synthetic or glass.

cards.q: What does fining do?
cards.explain: Agents like bentonite clay or egg white bind to particles, which settle out. Note: egg white and milk proteins mean some wines are not vegan.

cards.q: Tartrate crystals in a bottle are a serious fault.
cards.explain: Tartrates ('wine diamonds') are harmless. Cold stabilization prevents them for cosmetic reasons.

cards.q: Which closure best eliminates the risk of cork taint?
cards.explain: Screwcaps also keep aromatic whites fresh. They are standard in New Zealand and Australia.

cards.q: Match the vessel to its effect
cards.explain: The vessel is one of the winemaker's biggest stylistic choices.

cards.title: Yeast: wild or cultured
cards.body:
**Ambient** (wild) yeasts from the vineyard and cellar give complexity but can stall or make off-flavors. **Cultured** yeasts are reliable and can be chosen for aroma, speed or tolerance to alcohol.

Many top estates start with wild yeast and keep a cultured strain in reserve.

cards.title: Temperature and time
cards.body:
- **Cool** (12–16 °C) whites keep fruity esters: think Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling.
- **Warm** (25–32 °C) reds extract color and tannin quickly.
- **Extended maceration** after fermentation polymerizes tannins so they feel softer.
- **Cold soak** before fermentation extracts color and fruit without harsh tannin.

cards.title: Oxygen: friend and foe
cards.body:
**Reductive** winemaking keeps oxygen out (inert gas, sealed steel tanks, screw caps) for pure, fresh fruit.

**Oxidative** winemaking lets air in on purpose: barrels, racking, open vats, or the extreme cases of oloroso sherry and tawny port. A little oxygen softens tannin and builds complexity; too much makes wine flat and bruised-apple brown.

cards.title: Barrels in detail
cards.body:
- **Size**: a 225 L *barrique* gives more oak per liter than a 500 L *puncheon* or a 2,000 L *foudre*.
- **Age**: new oak gives the most flavor; after three or four fills it is almost neutral.
- **Origin**: French oak (tight grain: spice, toast, silkier) vs American oak (vanilla, coconut, dill).
- **Toast**: light (fresh wood, coconut) to heavy (coffee, smoke).

cards.title: Alternatives
cards.body:
**Concrete eggs**, **clay amphorae** and Georgia's buried **qvevri** let wine breathe without oak flavor. Georgia has made wine in qvevri for about 8,000 years; it is on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

Cheaper wines may use **oak chips or staves** in steel tanks for a fast oak note.

cards.q: Which barrel gives the strongest oak flavor?
cards.explain: Small and new means the most wood contact per liter and the most fresh oak compounds.

cards.q: What does reductive winemaking aim to do?
options: Keep oxygen away for pure, fresh fruit
cards.explain: Steel, inert gas and screw caps are the reductive toolkit.

cards.q: Match the vessel to its effect
pairs: Gentle oxygen with little oak flavor
cards.explain: The vessel shapes texture as much as flavor.

cards.q: American oak tends to show more coconut and vanilla than French oak.
cards.explain: It contains more of the lactones behind coconut aromas.

cards.title: Whole bunch and carbonic
cards.body: **Carbonic maceration** ferments whole, uncrushed grapes inside a CO₂-filled tank. The result is soft, very fruity, low-tannin red with notes of banana, bubblegum and kirsch: classic Beaujolais Nouveau.

cards.title: Fining, filtering, sulfur
cards.body:
Before bottling, wines are often **fined** (agents bind haze-causing particles) and **filtered**. A little **sulfur dioxide** protects against oxidation and microbes.

Some producers skip these steps for "natural" wines, accepting more risk and variation.

cards.q: Banana and bubblegum notes in a light red suggest…
cards.explain: Whole-berry fermentation creates these fruity esters, typical of Beaujolais Nouveau.

cards.q: Sulfur dioxide protects wine from oxidation.
cards.explain: SO₂ is an antioxidant and antimicrobial used in nearly all wines in small amounts.

cards.q: Match the technique to its result
cards.explain: Each technique targets one part of the finished wine.

cards.q: What is 'bâtonnage'?
cards.explain: Stirring dead yeast back into the wine adds body and a creamy, bready character.

cards.q: Adding sugar to the must to raise alcohol is called ___.
cards.explain: Chaptalization is allowed in some cool regions where grapes struggle to ripen.

units.title: Bordeaux
units.summary: Left Bank, Right Bank, the 1855 Classification and Sauternes.

cards.title: Gravel and Cabernet
cards.body:
West of the Gironde estuary and the Garonne river lie the **Médoc** and **Graves**. Deep **gravel** banks drain well and store heat, ideal for late-ripening **Cabernet Sauvignon**, which leads the blends.

The Haut-Médoc holds four famous communes, north to south: **Saint-Estèphe**, **Pauillac**, **Saint-Julien** and **Margaux**.

cards.title: The communes
cards.body:
- **Saint-Estèphe**: more clay, firmer, more rustic.
- **Pauillac**: powerful; three First Growths.
- **Saint-Julien**: balanced and consistent.
- **Margaux**: perfumed and silky.

cards.q: Which commune is home to three First Growths: Lafite, Latour and Mouton?
cards.explain: Pauillac is the heart of the Médoc's greatest Cabernet. The other First Growths are Château Margaux and Haut-Brion (Pessac-Léognan).

cards.q: Which is the northernmost of the four famous Haut-Médoc communes?
cards.explain: From north to south: Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux.

cards.q: Merlot is the dominant grape in most top Left Bank blends.
cards.explain: On the Left Bank, Cabernet Sauvignon usually leads. Merlot dominates on the Right Bank.

cards.q: Which Left Bank area makes both top reds and fine oaked dry whites?
cards.explain: It sits on the city's southern edge; Haut-Brion and Domaine de Chevalier make great reds and whites.

cards.title: Clay, limestone and Merlot
cards.body:
East of the Dordogne, cooler **clay and limestone** soils suit early-ripening **Merlot**, blended with **Cabernet Franc**.

- **Saint-Émilion**: a limestone plateau and slopes around a medieval town.
- **Pomerol**: a small clay-and-gravel plateau; Pétrus and Le Pin.
- Satellites: Fronsac, Castillon, Bourg, Blaye.

cards.title: Entre-Deux-Mers
cards.body: Between the Garonne and Dordogne lies **Entre-Deux-Mers**, best known for fresh, dry whites from Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon. Much of the region's generic Bordeaux AOC red comes from here too.

cards.q: Which grape partners Merlot on the Right Bank?
cards.explain: Cabernet Franc adds fragrance and structure. Château Cheval Blanc is famously Cabernet Franc-rich.

cards.q: Pomerol has an official classification of its châteaux.
cards.explain: Pomerol has no classification, yet Pétrus and Le Pin are among the most expensive wines in the world.

cards.q: 'Entre-Deux-Mers' means between two ___.
cards.explain: Poetically, the 'seas' are the tidal Garonne and Dordogne rivers.

cards.q: Match the soil to the grape it favors
cards.explain: Warm, free-draining gravel helps late Cabernet; cool, water-retentive clay suits early Merlot.

cards.title: 1855 and after
cards.body:
For the Paris Exposition of **1855**, Médoc châteaux (plus Haut-Brion) were ranked from **First** to **Fifth Growth**, based on price. Only one change has ever been made: **Mouton Rothschild** was promoted to First Growth in **1973**.

Sauternes was classified too, with **Château d'Yquem** alone as *Premier Cru Supérieur*. Saint-Émilion's classification is revised roughly every ten years.

cards.title: Sauternes
cards.body: Cool morning mists from the little **Ciron** river meet the warmer Garonne, encouraging **noble rot** on Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc. Pickers make several passes, choosing only botrytized berries.

cards.q: Which château was promoted to First Growth in 1973?
cards.explain: The only change ever made to the 1855 red classification.

cards.q: What was the 1855 Classification based on?
cards.explain: Brokers ranked châteaux by the prices their wines fetched at the time.

cards.q: Château d'Yquem holds the unique rank of Premier Cru Supérieur in Sauternes.
cards.explain: It was placed above all other Sauternes in 1855.

cards.q: Mists from the cool ___ river help noble rot develop in Sauternes.
cards.explain: Cold Ciron water meeting the warmer Garonne creates the autumn fog botrytis needs.

lessons.title: Deep dive: inside a Bordeaux château

cards.title: The blend
cards.body:
Bordeaux is a **blend** country. Five black grapes are allowed: **Cabernet Sauvignon** (structure, blackcurrant, age-worthiness), **Merlot** (plush plum, ripens early), **Cabernet Franc** (perfume, freshness), **Petit Verdot** (color, spice, a splash only) and **Malbec**. **Carmenère** is permitted but rare.

Blending is insurance: if one grape suffers from spring frost or autumn rain, the others carry the vintage.

cards.title: Grand vin and second wine
cards.body:
Each château makes its **grand vin** from the best plots and barrels. Lots that don't make the cut go into a **second wine**: Carruades de Lafite, Pavillon Rouge de Château Margaux, Les Forts de Latour.

Top grands vins spend **18–24 months** in barrels, often **mostly new French oak**, and are racked every few months to clear the sediment.

cards.title: En primeur
cards.body:
Every spring, merchants and critics taste the new vintage from barrel. Châteaux then release a part of the wine **en primeur**: buyers pay now and receive bottles about two years later.

Wine goes from château to *courtier* (broker) to *négociant* (merchant) to the world: the system known as **la Place de Bordeaux**.

cards.title: The Bordeaux bottle
cards.body:
The straight-sided bottle with **high shoulders** is the Bordeaux shape, copied worldwide for Cabernet and Merlot. The shoulders are said to catch sediment when pouring.

Large formats age more slowly; Bordeaux names them differently from Champagne: a **Double Magnum** holds 3 L and an **Impériale** 6 L.

cards.title: Dry whites and clairet
cards.body:
White Bordeaux blends **Sauvignon Blanc** (zest, grass) and **Sémillon** (wax, body, ageing), sometimes with Muscadelle. Simple Entre-Deux-Mers is fresh and unoaked; Pessac-Léognan whites are barrel-fermented and age for decades.

**Bordeaux clairet** is a deep rosé from a short maceration: the ancestor of the English word *claret*.

cards.q: What is a 'second wine' in Bordeaux?
options: Wine made from lots not chosen for the grand vin
A wine from the second harvest
A cheaper wine from another region
A wine aged a second year
cards.explain: Second wines give a taste of the house style at a lower price.

cards.q: Which grape gives Bordeaux blends their backbone and long ageing?
cards.explain: Its thick skins give firm tannin and blackcurrant fruit, especially on Left Bank gravel.

cards.q: En primeur means buying wine before it is bottled.
cards.explain: Buyers pay while the wine is still in barrel and receive it later.

cards.q: Match the Bordeaux grape to its role
cards.explain: Each grape plays a part; the blend changes every vintage.

cards.q: The English call red Bordeaux ___.
cards.explain: From the French clairet, the pale reds once shipped to England.

cards.title: Why vintages matter here
cards.body:
Bordeaux sits on the Atlantic: some years are warm and dry, others wet and cool. A great **vintage** needs a warm summer, a dry September and no rain at harvest.

Recent stars include **2005, 2009, 2010, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2020** and **2022**. In cooler years, Merlot on the Right Bank often does better than late-ripening Cabernet.

cards.title: How claret ages
cards.body:
Young top Bordeaux is **dark, tannic and oaky**: blackcurrant, cedar and vanilla.

After 10–20 years, tannins soften and **tertiary** notes appear: **cedar, cigar box, leather, forest floor, dried fruit**. The color fades from purple to **garnet** with a brick rim.

cards.title: Decanting
cards.body: Young claret benefits from **decanting** for air; old claret is decanted gently to leave its **sediment** behind. Stand the bottle upright a day before, then pour slowly over a light until the sediment reaches the neck.

cards.q: What does an aged Bordeaux typically smell of?
cards.explain: These tertiary notes come from years in bottle.

cards.q: In a cool, rainy Bordeaux vintage, which grape often fares better?
cards.explain: Merlot ripens earlier, so it can be picked before autumn rain.

cards.q: Old red wine is decanted partly to separate it from its sediment.
cards.explain: Tannins and pigments drop out as a fine deposit over the years.

cards.title: The 1855 Classification
cards.body:
In 1855, Médoc châteaux (plus Haut-Brion in Graves) were ranked into five growths by price. **First Growths**: Lafite, Latour, Margaux, Haut-Brion, and since 1973, Mouton Rothschild.

Sauternes was classified at the same time, with Yquem alone at the top.

cards.title: Bordeaux's dry whites and sweet wines
cards.body: Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon make crisp whites in Entre-Deux-Mers and serious oaked whites in Pessac-Léognan. In **Sauternes** and **Barsac**, autumn mists from the Ciron river bring noble rot for rich, honeyed sweet wines.

cards.q: Which château became a First Growth in 1973?
cards.explain: The only change ever made to the 1855 red classification.

cards.q: Pomerol has an official classification like the Médoc.
cards.explain: Pomerol has none, though Pétrus and Le Pin are among the world's most expensive wines.

cards.q: Match the appellation to its main grape
cards.explain: Left Bank leans Cabernet, Right Bank leans Merlot, sweet wines lean Sémillon.

cards.q: What brings noble rot to Sauternes?
options: Autumn mists from the Ciron river
cards.explain: Misty mornings and sunny afternoons are perfect for botrytis.

cards.q: Château ___ is the only Graves estate in the 1855 classification.
cards.explain: Haut-Brion was so famous in 1855 that it was included alongside the Médoc.

units.title: Burgundy & Beaujolais
units.summary: The Côte d'Or hierarchy, Chablis, the Mâconnais and the Beaujolais crus.

cards.title: The golden slope
cards.body:
A narrow, east-facing escarpment of limestone and marl south of Dijon.

- **Côte de Nuits** (north): almost all red. Gevrey-Chambertin, Chambolle-Musigny, Vougeot, Vosne-Romanée, Nuits-Saint-Georges.
- **Côte de Beaune** (south): great whites (Meursault, Puligny- and Chassagne-Montrachet) and reds (Pommard, Volnay, Corton).

cards.title: The quality pyramid
cards.body:
- **Grand Cru** (33 vineyards; names like Le Chambertin or Le Montrachet appear alone on the label)
- **Premier Cru** (village + vineyard, e.g. Meursault 1er Cru Perrières)
- **Village** (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin)
- **Regional** (Bourgogne)

The best sites sit mid-slope, with ideal drainage and sun.

cards.q: Which half of the Côte d'Or is most famous for white wine?
cards.explain: Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne make the world's most revered Chardonnay.

cards.q: Approximately how many Grand Cru vineyards does Burgundy have?
cards.explain: Together they make only about 1–2% of Burgundy's wine.

cards.q: In the Côte d'Or, the finest vineyards are usually at the bottom of the slope.
cards.explain: Mid-slope sites usually have the best balance of drainage, soil depth and sun.

cards.q: Match the wine to its part of Burgundy
cards.explain: The Côte de Nuits is red country; the great whites shine in the southern Côte de Beaune; the Mâconnais and Chalonnaise offer value.

cards.title: Chablis
cards.body:
Far to the north-west, on **Kimmeridgian** limestone rich in fossilized oyster shells. Chardonnay here is **steely**, with green apple, lemon and wet stones. Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and **seven Grand Cru** climats on one slope.

Frost is the big risk, fought with heaters and sprinklers.

cards.title: Chalonnaise & Mâconnais
cards.body:
- **Côte Chalonnaise**: Mercurey, Givry, Rully, Montagny. Value Burgundy.
- **Mâconnais**: warmer and riper Chardonnay: Mâcon-Villages, **Pouilly-Fuissé**, **Saint-Véran**.

cards.q: The soil of Chablis is famous for…
options: Kimmeridgian limestone with fossil oyster shells
cards.explain: Many link its minerality to these ancient marine soils, also found in Sancerre and the Côte des Bar.

cards.q: Pouilly-Fuissé is a Chardonnay from the Mâconnais.
cards.explain: Don't confuse it with Pouilly-Fumé, a Sauvignon Blanc from the Loire.

cards.q: What is the main climatic threat in Chablis?
cards.explain: Being far north, Chablis often loses buds to spring frost.

cards.q: Chablis has ___ Grand Cru climats, all on a single slope.
cards.explain: Including Les Clos, Vaudésir and Valmur, on a south-west-facing hill above the town.

cards.title: Gamay on granite
cards.body:
Granite hills in the north, clay and limestone in the south.

- **Beaujolais** and **Nouveau**: light, fruity, often carbonic.
- **Beaujolais-Villages**: a step up.
- **The ten crus** (Fleurie, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent and more): more structure; some age for a decade.

cards.q: How many Beaujolais crus are there?
cards.explain: From north to south: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly.

cards.q: Beaujolais crus usually show the word 'Beaujolais' prominently on the label.
cards.explain: Crus usually just show the village name, such as Morgon or Fleurie.

cards.q: Which cru is known for the most powerful, age-worthy Beaujolais?
cards.explain: Named after its windmill. Its manganese-rich granite gives structured, long-lived wines.

cards.q: Most Beaujolais lies on ___ soils in the northern hills.
cards.explain: Granite gives the crus their structure and floral perfume.

cards.title: Four levels
cards.body:
Burgundy ranks **land**, not producers:

1. **Grand Cru** (about 1% of wine): named vineyards only, such as *Chambertin*, *Montrachet*, *Corton*.
2. **Premier Cru** (about 10%): village + vineyard, *Gevrey-Chambertin 1er Cru Clos Saint-Jacques*.
3. **Village** (about 37%): *Meursault*, *Vosne-Romanée*.
4. **Regional** (about half): *Bourgogne*, *Mâcon-Villages*.

cards.title: Climats and clos
cards.body:
A named vineyard plot is a **climat**; there are over 1,200, listed by UNESCO since 2015. A **clos** is a vineyard enclosed by a stone wall, often built by medieval monks.

Because of Napoleonic inheritance laws, one vineyard is usually split between **many owners**: Clos de Vougeot's 50 hectares have around 80.

cards.title: Domaine or négociant
cards.body:
A **domaine** grows and bottles its own grapes. A **négociant** (merchant house such as Louis Jadot, Joseph Drouhin, Bouchard) buys grapes or wine and bottles under its name.

So the same vineyard name can appear on dozens of different labels: the producer matters as much as the plot.

cards.title: How red Burgundy is made
cards.body:
Pinot Noir is thin-skinned and delicate. Winemakers often do a **cold soak** before fermentation for color, use gentle **punch-downs**, and may keep some **whole bunches** for perfume.

It ages 12–18 months in French oak *pièces* (228 L barrels); the share of new oak rises with the quality level.

cards.title: The Burgundy bottle
cards.body: The Burgundy bottle has **sloping shoulders** and a wider body, the shape used worldwide for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay (and in the Rhône for Syrah).

cards.q: Which is the top level of the Burgundy hierarchy?
cards.explain: Grand Cru wines carry only the vineyard name, like Romanée-Conti or Le Montrachet.

cards.q: What is a 'clos'?
cards.explain: Clos de Vougeot and Clos de Tart are famous examples.

cards.q: In Burgundy, one vineyard is often shared by many owners.
cards.explain: Inheritance laws split plots over generations; some owners have just a few rows.

cards.q: Match the label to its level
cards.explain: More specific place = higher level.

cards.title: Chablis on Kimmeridgian clay
cards.body:
Chablis is cool and isolated, nearer to Champagne than to Beaune. Its best slopes sit on **Kimmeridgian** marl full of tiny fossilized oyster shells.

Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru, and **seven Grands Crus** on one south-west-facing hill above the town (Les Clos, Vaudésir, Blanchot…). Most is unoaked; some Grands Crus use old oak.

cards.title: Beaujolais and carbonic maceration
cards.body:
**Gamay** on granite hills south of Mâcon. For juicy, fruity styles, whole bunches are sealed in tanks full of carbon dioxide: fermentation starts **inside each berry** (**carbonic maceration**), giving banana, bubblegum and kirsch notes and low tannin.

**Beaujolais Nouveau** is released on the third Thursday of November. The **ten crus** (Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie…) are deeper and can age.

cards.q: What makes Chablis' best soils special?
options: Kimmeridgian marl with fossil oyster shells
cards.explain: It is linked with Chablis' steely, saline character.

cards.q: What is carbonic maceration?
cards.explain: In a CO2-filled tank, enzymes start fermenting each berry from the inside.

cards.q: Chablis has seven Grand Cru vineyards, all on one hillside.
cards.explain: They face south-west across the Serein river from the town.

cards.title: The Côte d'Or
cards.body: The **Côte de Nuits** (north) is mostly red Pinot Noir: Gevrey-Chambertin, Vosne-Romanée, Chambolle-Musigny. The **Côte de Beaune** (south) is famous for whites: Meursault, Puligny- and Chassagne-Montrachet, plus reds from Pommard and Volnay.

cards.title: Climats
cards.body: Burgundy is divided into hundreds of named plots called **climats**, recognized by UNESCO. Many are split between several owners, so the producer matters as much as the vineyard.

cards.q: Which village is in the Côte de Beaune?
cards.explain: Meursault is a great white-wine village of the Côte de Beaune.

cards.q: The Côte de Nuits is best known for red wines.
cards.explain: Nearly all its Grand Crus are Pinot Noir; Musigny has a tiny white exception.

cards.q: Match the Grand Cru to its color
cards.explain: Côte de Beaune Grand Crus are mostly white; Côte de Nuits mostly red.

cards.q: Why does the producer matter so much in Burgundy?
options: Many vineyards are split between owners
cards.explain: Clos de Vougeot alone has more than 80 owners, each making different wine.

cards.q: Burgundy's named vineyard plots are called ___.
cards.explain: The climats of Burgundy became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.

units.title: Rhône, Loire, Alsace & Champagne
units.summary: France beyond Bordeaux and Burgundy, in depth.

cards.title: Two different worlds
cards.body:
- **Northern Rhône**: moderate continental climate, steep **granite** terraces, **Syrah** alone (sometimes with a little white grape co-fermented). Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage, Cornas, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, plus Viognier in Condrieu.
- **Southern Rhône**: Mediterranean heat, the **Mistral** wind, **Grenache**-led blends. Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Côtes du Rhône, Tavel rosé.

cards.q: What is the Mistral?
options: A cold, dry wind in the Southern Rhône
cards.explain: It reduces disease pressure and can damage vines, so many old vines are trained as low bush vines.

cards.q: Which Northern Rhône appellation may include Viognier co-fermented with Syrah?
cards.explain: Up to 20% Viognier is allowed, adding perfume and stabilizing color, though most use far less.

cards.q: Châteauneuf-du-Pape's galets roulés are large stones that store and radiate heat.
cards.explain: Rounded quartzite pebbles cover many vineyards, helping Grenache ripen.

cards.q: Match the appellation to its style
cards.explain: North for single varietals; south for blends and rosé.

cards.title: Four sections
cards.body:
- **Pays Nantais**: Muscadet (Melon de Bourgogne), maritime.
- **Anjou-Saumur**: Chenin (dry Savennières, sweet Coteaux du Layon), Cabernet Franc, sparkling Saumur.
- **Touraine**: Vouvray, Montlouis, Chinon, Bourgueil.
- **Central Vineyards**: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé (Sauvignon Blanc).

cards.q: Which Loire sub-region is closest to the Atlantic?
cards.explain: Around Nantes. Its maritime climate suits Muscadet.

cards.q: Coteaux du Layon is known for…
cards.explain: Autumn mists along the Layon river encourage noble rot. Quarts de Chaume and Bonnezeaux are top crus.

cards.q: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé face each other across the Loire.
cards.explain: Sancerre on the west bank, Pouilly-sur-Loire on the east.

cards.q: Pouilly-___ is a Loire Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-Fuissé is a Burgundy Chardonnay.
cards.explain: A classic exam trap!

cards.title: Sheltered and dry
cards.body:
The **Vosges mountains** cast a rain shadow, making Alsace one of France's driest, sunniest regions. Wines are labeled by grape: **Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat** (the four 'noble' grapes for Grand Cru), plus Pinot Blanc and Pinot Noir.

Special sweet styles: **Vendanges Tardives** (late harvest) and **Sélection de Grains Nobles** (botrytis).

cards.q: Why is Alsace so dry and sunny for its latitude?
options: The Vosges mountains create a rain shadow
cards.explain: Westerly rain falls on the mountains, leaving the eastern foothills dry.

cards.q: Alsace wines are usually labeled by grape variety.
cards.explain: Unusually for France, the grape name is front and center, in tall flûte bottles.

cards.q: Sélection de Grains Nobles means…
cards.explain: Made from individually selected noble-rot berries, rich and luscious.

cards.q: Match the Alsace grape to its style
cards.explain: Muscat in Alsace is usually dry and grapey.

cards.title: Assemblage and house style
cards.body:
Champagne is about **blending** (assemblage): grapes, villages and **reserve wines** from older vintages create a consistent non-vintage house style.

Villages are rated: **17 Grand Cru** and **42 Premier Cru**. Growers' own Champagnes ('grower Champagne') bear **RM** on the label; big houses use **NM**.

cards.title: Sweetness ladder
cards.body: From driest: **Brut Nature** (0–3 g/L), **Extra Brut**, **Brut** (under 12), **Extra Dry**, **Sec**, **Demi-Sec**, **Doux** (over 50).

cards.q: What do reserve wines give non-vintage Champagne?
cards.explain: Older wines blended in smooth out vintage variation and add depth.

cards.q: Which is the driest sweetness term?
cards.explain: No sugar added at dosage, 0–3 g/L.

cards.q: 'RM' on a Champagne label means the grower made the wine from their own grapes.
cards.explain: Récoltant-Manipulant. NM (Négociant-Manipulant) is a house that buys grapes.

cards.q: Champagne has ___ Grand Cru villages.
cards.explain: Including Aÿ, Bouzy, Cramant, Avize and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger.

lessons.title: Deep dive: the Rhône, north and south

cards.title: Northern Rhône: Syrah on granite
cards.body:
A narrow valley of steep **granite** terraces. **Syrah** is the only black grape, giving black pepper, blackberry, olive and violet.

- **Côte-Rôtie**: may co-ferment up to 20% **Viognier** for perfume.
- **Hermitage**: one south-facing hill, the most powerful and long-lived.
- **Cornas**: 100% Syrah, wild and tannic. **Crozes-Hermitage** and **Saint-Joseph**: larger, more affordable.
- **Condrieu**: 100% Viognier white, apricot and blossom.

cards.title: Southern Rhône: the GSM blend
cards.body:
A wide, sunny plain swept by the cold **mistral** wind. Reds are blends led by **Grenache**, with **Syrah** (color, pepper) and **Mourvèdre** (structure, meaty depth): **GSM**.

**Châteauneuf-du-Pape** allows 13 varieties; its vineyards are covered in big rounded stones, the **galets roulés**. The papal coat of arms is embossed on many bottles. Neighbors: **Gigondas**, **Vacqueyras**, **Tavel** (rosé only), and great-value **Côtes du Rhône**.

cards.q: What is the only black grape of the northern Rhône?
cards.explain: Grenache-led blends belong to the south.

cards.q: What does GSM stand for?
cards.explain: The classic southern Rhône blend, copied in Australia's McLaren Vale and Barossa.

cards.q: Côte-Rôtie may include some white Viognier in its red wine.
cards.explain: Co-fermenting a little Viognier lifts aroma and stabilizes color.

cards.q: Match the appellation to its wine
cards.explain: Rhône appellations each have a signature.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Loire, Alsace and Champagne houses

cards.title: The Loire: four grapes, one river
cards.body:
From the Atlantic inland: **Muscadet** (Melon, sur lie), **Anjou-Saumur** (Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc, sweet Coteaux du Layon), **Touraine** (Vouvray Chenin, Chinon Cabernet Franc), and the **Centre** (**Sancerre** and **Pouilly-Fumé**, Sauvignon Blanc).

Chenin Blanc can be bone dry, sparkling, or lusciously sweet, sometimes from the same village.

cards.title: Alsace: French wines, German grapes
cards.body:
Sheltered by the Vosges mountains, Alsace is one of France's **driest** regions. Wines are labeled by **grape**, unusual for France: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat are the four "noble" ones, with 51 **Grands Crus**.

Wines come in the tall, slender **flûte** bottle. *Vendanges Tardives* (late harvest) and *Sélection de Grains Nobles* (botrytis) are the sweet styles. Most wines skip new oak and many skip malolactic conversion to keep acidity.

cards.title: Champagne's great houses
cards.body:
Big houses (*grandes marques*) aim for a consistent **non-vintage** style year after year by blending many villages and **reserve wines** from older years.

Prestige *cuvées* are their flagships: Dom Pérignon (Moët), Cristal (Roederer), La Grande Dame (Veuve Clicquot). Krug and Bollinger ferment in oak; Ruinart is known for Chardonnay.

cards.q: How are Alsace wines usually labeled?
cards.explain: Alsace is the main French region that puts the grape front and center.

cards.q: Which Loire grape makes Vouvray?
cards.explain: Vouvray can be sec, demi-sec, moelleux or sparkling.

cards.q: Reserve wines help Champagne houses keep a consistent non-vintage style.
cards.explain: Older wines are blended in to smooth out differences between years.

cards.title: Champagne houses and growers
cards.body: Big **houses** (négociants) buy grapes from many villages and blend for a consistent house style. **Grower Champagnes** come from a single estate's own vines, showing their village's character. Look for "RM" (récoltant-manipulant) on the label.

cards.title: The Loire's many faces
cards.body: From the Atlantic inland: **Muscadet** (Melon), **Anjou-Saumur** (Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc), **Touraine** (Vouvray Chenin, Chinon Cabernet Franc) and the **Centre** (Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé Sauvignon Blanc).

cards.q: What does 'RM' on a Champagne label mean?
options: A grower making wine from their own grapes
cards.explain: Récoltant-manipulant: the same family grows, makes and bottles the wine.

cards.q: Match the Loire wine to its grape
cards.explain: The Loire grows mostly single varieties, each in its own district.

cards.q: Alsace wines are usually labeled with the grape variety.
cards.explain: Unusually for France, Alsace names the grape: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris.

cards.q: Which southern French region is known for Grenache-based Banyuls and Côtes du Roussillon?
cards.explain: Next to the Pyrenees, Roussillon makes powerful reds and sweet fortified Banyuls and Maury.

cards.q: Jura's oxidative 'yellow wine' is called vin ___.
cards.explain: Vin jaune ages under a yeast veil for over six years, like a French cousin of Fino sherry.

units.title: Italy
units.summary: Piedmont, Tuscany, the North East and the South.

cards.title: The Langhe
cards.body:
Fog-wrapped hills around **Alba**. Continental climate; best sites face south.

- **Barolo**: Nebbiolo, minimum 38 months' ageing (18 in wood). Powerful, structured.
- **Barbaresco**: Nebbiolo, 26 months. Often more elegant.
- **Barbera d'Asti** and **Dolcetto d'Alba**: everyday reds.
- **Moscato d'Asti**: gently sparkling and sweet. **Gavi**: crisp Cortese.

cards.q: What is the minimum ageing for Barolo?
cards.explain: Including 18 months in wood. Riserva requires 62 months.

cards.q: Which Piedmont grape is deeply colored with high acidity but low tannin?
cards.explain: Barbera's juicy acidity and soft tannin make it a perfect food wine.

cards.q: Barbaresco is made from Sangiovese.
cards.explain: Barbaresco, like Barolo, is 100% Nebbiolo.

cards.q: Gavi is a crisp white wine from the ___ grape.
cards.explain: Lemon, green apple and almond; a classic with pesto from nearby Liguria.

cards.title: Sangiovese country
cards.body:
- **Chianti Classico**: the historic heart (black rooster symbol), ≥80% Sangiovese. Annata → Riserva → **Gran Selezione**.
- **Brunello di Montalcino**: 100% Sangiovese, released five years after harvest.
- **Vino Nobile di Montepulciano**: Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile).
- **Bolgheri**: coastal Super Tuscans from Bordeaux varieties.

cards.q: Brunello di Montalcino is made from…
cards.explain: A local clone called Brunello. Warm, dry Montalcino gives power and longevity.

cards.q: What is a Super Tuscan?
options: A Tuscan wine made outside traditional rules
cards.explain: Starting with Sassicaia and Tignanello in the 1970s, often with Cabernet or Merlot, first released as table wine.

cards.q: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is made from the Montepulciano grape.
cards.explain: It's Sangiovese from the town of Montepulciano. The Montepulciano grape is grown in Abruzzo.

cards.q: Match the Tuscan wine to its place
cards.explain: Three of Tuscany's great names.

cards.title: Veneto and beyond
cards.body:
- **Valpolicella** (Corvina): light Valpolicella, **Ripasso**, dry **Amarone** and sweet **Recioto** from dried grapes (appassimento).
- **Soave** (Garganega). **Prosecco** (Glera).
- **Friuli**: fine whites and orange wines. **Alto Adige**: Alpine aromatic whites.

cards.q: How is Amarone made?
options: From grapes dried for months before fermentation
cards.explain: Appassimento concentrates sugar; fermenting to dryness gives a powerful wine of about 15–16% abv.

cards.q: Ripasso is Valpolicella refermented on leftover Amarone skins.
cards.explain: It adds body, alcohol and dried-fruit flavor: 'baby Amarone'.

cards.q: Soave is made mainly from the ___ grape.
cards.explain: From volcanic and limestone hills east of Verona.

cards.q: Which Italian region is known for skin-contact orange wines?
cards.explain: Pioneers near the Slovenian border revived long skin maceration for white grapes such as Ribolla Gialla.

cards.title: Volcanoes and sunshine
cards.body:
- **Campania**: Taurasi (Aglianico), Fiano di Avellino, Greco di Tufo.
- **Basilicata**: Aglianico del Vulture.
- **Puglia**: Primitivo and Negroamaro.
- **Sicily**: Nero d'Avola, and elegant Etna wines (Nerello Mascalese, Carricante) from volcanic slopes.
- **Sardinia**: Cannonau (Grenache) and Vermentino.

cards.q: Taurasi is made from…
cards.explain: Often called the Barolo of the South, high in tannin and acidity.

cards.q: Cannonau, from Sardinia, is the same grape as Grenache.
cards.explain: Sardinia has a long tradition of the grape, possibly as old as Spain's.

cards.q: Why are Mount Etna's wines fresher than much of Sicily's?
cards.explain: Vineyards climb above 1,000 m, giving cool nights and elegant wines.

cards.q: Match the southern grape to its region
cards.explain: Three of southern Italy's most important grapes.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Piedmont and Tuscany up close

cards.title: Barolo and Barbaresco
cards.body:
In the **Langhe** hills near Alba, **Nebbiolo** ripens late, often picked in October fog (*nebbia*). It is pale in color but high in **tannin and acidity**, smelling of **roses, tar, cherry and licorice**.

**Barolo**: at least 38 months of ageing (18 in wood), 62 months for Riserva. **Barbaresco**: at least 26 months. Single vineyards are labeled as **MGA** (*menzioni geografiche aggiuntive*), like Cannubi or Rabajà.

cards.title: Traditionalists vs modernists
cards.body:
In the 1980s–90s the "Barolo wars" split producers: **traditionalists** used long macerations and big old casks (*botti*); **modernists** used short macerations and new French *barriques* for softer, oakier wines.

Today most producers sit in between.

cards.title: Chianti Classico and Brunello
cards.body:
**Sangiovese** loves Tuscany's hills: sour cherry, tomato leaf, dried herbs, high acidity.

- **Chianti Classico**: the historic zone, black rooster on the neck; Annata, Riserva and **Gran Selezione** (top tier).
- **Brunello di Montalcino**: 100% Sangiovese, released five years after harvest.
- **Vino Nobile di Montepulciano**: the town, not the grape.
- **Super Tuscans**: Bordeaux varieties on the coast at **Bolgheri** (Sassicaia, Ornellaia), first sold as humble *vino da tavola*.

cards.title: The Italian pyramid
cards.body:
- **DOCG**: the top, with a numbered neck strip (Barolo, Brunello, Chianti Classico…).
- **DOC**: controlled origin.
- **IGT**: regional wine with freer rules: where many Super Tuscans began.
- **Vino**: table wine.

cards.q: Which grape makes Barolo and Barbaresco?
cards.explain: Named after the fog (nebbia) of harvest time.

cards.q: What symbol marks Chianti Classico?
cards.explain: The gallo nero has been the consortium's emblem for nearly a century.

cards.q: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is made from the Montepulciano grape.
cards.explain: It is Sangiovese from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano. The grape Montepulciano grows in Abruzzo.

cards.q: Match the Italian wine to its grape
cards.explain: Italy's great wines rest on native grapes.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Veneto, the South and the islands

cards.title: Amarone and appassimento
cards.body:
In Valpolicella, **Corvina** grapes are dried for about **100 days** in lofts (*fruttai*), losing a third or more of their weight. Fermented dry, they make **Amarone**: 15–16% alcohol, raisin, cherry and chocolate. Fermentation stopped early gives sweet **Recioto**.

**Ripasso** re-passes young Valpolicella over Amarone skins for extra body.

cards.title: The South awakens
cards.body:
- **Campania**: **Aglianico** in Taurasi (the "Barolo of the South"), whites **Fiano di Avellino** and **Greco di Tufo**.
- **Puglia**: rich **Primitivo** (Zinfandel) and **Negroamaro**.
- **Sicily**: **Nero d'Avola**, and on volcanic **Etna**, elegant Nerello Mascalese reds and Carricante whites at up to 1,000 m.
- **Sardinia**: **Vermentino** and **Cannonau** (Grenache).

cards.q: How long are grapes typically dried for Amarone?
cards.explain: Drying concentrates sugar and flavor; the wine is fermented to dryness.

cards.q: Primitivo from Puglia is genetically the same as…
cards.explain: Both trace back to the Croatian grape Crljenak Kaštelanski (Tribidrag).

cards.q: Cannonau, Sardinia's main red grape, is Grenache.
cards.explain: Sardinians claim it as their own; it is the same variety as Garnacha.

cards.title: Super Tuscans
cards.body: In the 1970s, producers like Sassicaia and Tignanello broke DOC rules, using Cabernet Sauvignon and French oak. Sold as simple table wine, they became famous as **Super Tuscans**, and Bolgheri later got its own DOC.

cards.title: The Veneto
cards.body: **Valpolicella** blends Corvina with other local grapes. **Amarone** is made from grapes dried for months (appassimento), giving rich, high-alcohol, dry reds. **Ripasso** passes young Valpolicella over Amarone skins for extra body.

cards.q: What is 'appassimento'?
cards.explain: Drying concentrates sugar and flavor; it's how Amarone and Recioto are made.

cards.q: Match the wine to its region
cards.explain: Italy's twenty regions each have their own grapes and wines.

cards.q: Super Tuscans often include Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot.
cards.explain: International grapes are what made them break the old rules.

cards.q: Which grape is the backbone of Valpolicella and Amarone?
cards.explain: Corvina gives sour cherry and almond notes and dries well for Amarone.

cards.q: Sassicaia comes from the coastal Tuscan zone of ___.
cards.explain: Bolgheri, near the coast, became famous for Bordeaux-style blends.

units.title: Spain & Portugal
units.summary: Rioja and Ribera, Spain's diverse regions, and Portugal from Vinho Verde to the Douro.

cards.title: Rioja
cards.body:
Along the **Ebro**, sheltered by mountains. Three zones: cooler **Rioja Alta** and **Rioja Alavesa**, warmer **Rioja Oriental**.

**Tempranillo** leads, with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo (Carignan). Traditional producers age long in American oak; modern ones use French oak, riper fruit and single vineyards.

cards.title: Ribera del Duero
cards.body: A high plateau (about 750–850 m) along the Duero. Hot days and very cold nights produce deep, powerful **Tinto Fino** (Tempranillo). Vega Sicilia and Pingus are icons.

cards.q: Which Rioja zone is the warmest?
cards.explain: Lower and more Mediterranean, it suits Garnacha.

cards.q: Ribera del Duero's vineyards are at high altitude, giving cold nights.
cards.explain: Frost is a risk, but the diurnal range keeps acidity and color.

cards.q: Mazuelo, used in Rioja, is better known as…
cards.explain: Also called Cariñena in Spain. It adds acidity and color to blends.

cards.q: A red Rioja Reserva must age at least ___ years, one in oak.
cards.explain: Crianza needs two years (one in oak); Gran Reserva needs five (two in oak).

cards.title: From Galicia to Andalucía
cards.body:
- **Rías Baixas**: Albariño. **Rueda**: Verdejo. **Bierzo**: Mencía.
- **Priorat**: old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena on llicorella slate.
- **Penedès**: Cava (Macabeo, Xarel·lo, Parellada).
- **La Mancha**: the huge central plain. **Jumilla**: Monastrell.
- **Jerez**: Sherry.

cards.q: Priorat's famous slate soil is called…
cards.explain: Dark, crumbly slate that forces roots deep and gives low yields of intense wine. Albariza is the white chalk of Jerez.

cards.q: Match the Spanish region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Spain is far more than Tempranillo.

cards.q: Albariza is the chalky white soil of the Sherry region.
cards.explain: It holds winter rain like a sponge and bakes into a hard crust in summer.

cards.q: Which grapes make Cava?
cards.explain: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are also permitted.

cards.title: The Douro and beyond
cards.body:
- **Vinho Verde**: rainy north-west; fresh, light whites, Alvarinho at its best.
- **Douro**: hot schist terraces; Port and powerful dry reds from Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz.
- **Dão**: granite plateau, elegant reds. **Bairrada**: Baga.
- **Alentejo**: hot plains; ripe reds; cork forests.

cards.q: The Douro's vineyards grow on…
cards.explain: The schist breaks into layers that let vine roots dig deep for water in the hot, dry summers.

cards.q: Portugal is the world's largest producer of cork.
cards.explain: Most of it comes from cork oak forests in the Alentejo.

cards.q: Which grape is considered Portugal's finest black variety?
cards.explain: Deep, floral and structured, it is key to both Port and Douro reds.

cards.q: LBV Port stands for Late Bottled ___.
cards.explain: Single-vintage Port aged 4–6 years in wood, ready to drink sooner than Vintage Port.

cards.title: Rioja's ageing ladder
cards.body:
Rioja splits into **Rioja Alta**, **Rioja Alavesa** (cooler, higher) and **Rioja Oriental** (warmer, more Garnacha). **Tempranillo** leads, with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo (Carignan).

Labels show **time in oak and bottle** (red minimums):
- **Joven**: little or no oak.
- **Crianza**: 2 years, at least 1 in oak.
- **Reserva**: 3 years, at least 1 in oak.
- **Gran Reserva**: 5 years, at least 2 in oak.

Traditional bodegas use **American oak**: vanilla, coconut, dill.

cards.title: The new Spain
cards.body:
- **Ribera del Duero**: Tempranillo (Tinto Fino) on a high plateau; Vega Sicilia, Pingus.
- **Priorat**: old Garnacha and Cariñena on black slate (*llicorella*); one of only two **DOCa** with Rioja.
- **Rías Baixas**: Albariño by the Atlantic.
- **Bierzo**: Mencía, fresh and floral.
- **Toro** and **Jumilla** (Monastrell): power and sun.

cards.q: Which Rioja label means at least 5 years of ageing?
cards.explain: Gran Reserva reds age at least 5 years, 2 of them in oak.

cards.q: What is llicorella?
cards.explain: The broken black slate forces roots deep and gives low yields.

cards.q: Match the Spanish region to its grape
cards.explain: Spain is far more than Tempranillo.

cards.q: Traditional Rioja is often aged in American oak.
cards.explain: It gives the classic vanilla and coconut notes.

cards.title: Over 250 native grapes
cards.body:
Portugal kept its own grapes when much of the world planted French ones.

- **Touriga Nacional**: violet, black fruit, the star of Port and Douro reds.
- **Touriga Franca**, **Tinta Roriz** (Tempranillo), **Baga** (Bairrada's tannic red).
- **Alvarinho** and **Loureiro** in Vinho Verde; **Encruzado** in Dão; **Arinto** everywhere for acidity.

cards.title: Regions to know
cards.body:
- **Vinho Verde**: light, fresh, sometimes spritzy whites.
- **Douro**: Port, and now great dry reds from the same terraces.
- **Dão**: granite hills, elegant reds.
- **Bairrada**: Baga reds and traditional-method sparkling.
- **Alentejo**: hot plains, ripe reds; some still fermented in clay **talhas**.
- **Setúbal**: sweet fortified Moscatel.

cards.q: Which grape is considered Portugal's finest red?
cards.explain: Deep color, violet perfume and structure: used in Port and dry Douro reds.

cards.q: What are talhas?
cards.explain: A Roman-era tradition revived under the Vinho de Talha DOC.

cards.q: Tinta Roriz is Portugal's name for Tempranillo.
cards.explain: It is also called Aragonez in the Alentejo.

cards.title: Rioja's subregions
cards.body: Rioja has three parts: **Rioja Alta** (cooler, elegant), **Rioja Alavesa** (limestone, finesse) and **Rioja Oriental** (warmer, Garnacha-rich). Traditional producers age in American oak; modern ones favor French oak and riper fruit.

cards.title: Port styles
cards.body: **Ruby** and **Vintage** Port age mostly in bottle and stay deep red with black fruit. **Tawny** ages in small casks, turning amber with nutty, caramel notes; 10, 20, 30 and 40 Year Old labels give an average age.

cards.q: Which Port style ages in small casks and turns amber?
cards.explain: Oxygen through the wood gives Tawny its color and nutty, caramel character.

cards.q: Match the Spanish region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Spain's regions each lean on a local hero grape.

cards.q: American oak gives stronger coconut and vanilla notes than French oak.
cards.explain: That's why traditional Rioja often smells of vanilla and coconut.

cards.q: What does '20 Year Old' on a Tawny Port mean?
options: A blend with an average age of about 20 years
Every drop is exactly 20 years old
It must be drunk within 20 years
cards.explain: Indicated-age Tawnies are blends that taste like the stated age.

cards.q: Priorat's dark slate and quartz soil is called ___.
cards.explain: Llicorella forces vine roots deep and gives Priorat its mineral intensity.

units.title: Germany, Austria, Hungary & Greece
units.summary: Prädikat levels, Austrian classics, Tokaji and Greece's revival.

cards.title: Ripeness levels
cards.body:
German **Prädikatswein** is classified by grape sugar at harvest:

- **Kabinett**: light, often off-dry.
- **Spätlese**: late harvest, riper.
- **Auslese**: selected bunches.
- **Beerenauslese (BA)**: selected berries, often botrytized.
- **Eiswein**: frozen grapes.
- **Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA)**: shriveled botrytized berries.

A ripeness level is not a sweetness level: a Spätlese can be **trocken** (dry).

cards.q: Which Prädikat is made from individually picked shriveled, botrytized berries?
cards.explain: TBA is one of the world's rarest, sweetest wines, sometimes with under 6% alcohol.

cards.q: A Spätlese is always sweet.
cards.explain: Spätlese means late harvest, a ripeness level. It can be fermented dry (Spätlese trocken).

cards.q: Which region is famous for delicate, low-alcohol Riesling on steep slate?
cards.explain: The Mosel's blue and red slate slopes are among the steepest vineyards in the world.

cards.q: Match the German region to its specialty
cards.explain: Germany's warmest region (Baden) excels with the Pinot family.

cards.title: Precision and purity
cards.body:
- **Niederösterreich**: Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal: Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.
- **Wachau** ripeness categories: **Steinfeder** (light), **Federspiel**, **Smaragd** (richest).
- **Burgenland**: Blaufränkisch, Zweigelt and sweet wines around Lake Neusiedl.
- **Steiermark**: Sauvignon Blanc.

**DAC** labels show typical regional styles.

cards.q: In the Wachau, the ripest dry style is called…
cards.explain: Named after an emerald-green lizard that basks on the warm terraces.

cards.q: Lake Neusiedl's humidity helps produce botrytized sweet wines.
cards.explain: Morning mists from the shallow lake encourage noble rot.

cards.q: Austria's most planted red grape is…
cards.explain: A 1922 cross of St. Laurent and Blaufränkisch.

cards.q: DAC stands for Districtus Austriae ___.
cards.explain: It marks wines typical of their region.

cards.title: Tokaji
cards.body:
In north-east **Hungary**, volcanic hills and river mists favor noble rot on **Furmint** and Hárslevelű.

- **Tokaji Aszú**: aszú berries macerated in base wine; at least 120 g/L sugar.
- **Eszencia**: the free-run syrup of aszú berries; can be 500+ g/L sugar and as low as 3% alcohol.
- Increasingly fine **dry Furmint**.

cards.title: Greece
cards.body:
